sentence: A band neutrophil has an elongated, narrow band-shaped nucleus of uniform thickness with a singular lobe, whereas a segmented neutrophil has a nucleus with 2 to 5 lobes connected by thin filaments [2][3].
Both cell types are similar in size (10-16 microns) and have abundant pink cytoplasm with specific granules, but the key distinguishing feature is the nuclear morphology.
The segmented neutrophil's nucleus is multilobed, while the band neutrophil's nucleus is unsegmented and shaped like a band [2][3][4].

Toxic changes in neutrophils on a film include toxic granulation, which appears as dark blue-black peroxidase-positive granules in the cytoplasm, toxic vacuolation seen as clear, circular unstained areas, and Dohle bodies, which are pale blue, round or elongated cytoplasmic inclusions containing remnant RNA [1].
These features are typically observed in mature neutrophils and bands, often alongside a left shift with increased immature granulocytes [1].
A hypersegmented neutrophil has two to five lobes and is a diagnostic feature of megaloblastic anemia [1].
It may also be associated with familial conditions, iron deficiency anemia, or renal failure [1].

Smudge cells are often the result of fragile leukocytes, such as lymphocytes or neutrophils, rupturing during smear preparation, which creates artifacts that appear as naked nuclei or cell fragments [1][2].
In conditions like chronic lymphocytic leukemia (CLL), numerous small mature lymphocytes are prone to rupture, leading to a high number of smudge cells [4].
Additionally, in infections, neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs) can resemble smudge cells and may contribute to their abundance, especially when NET formation is increased [2][3][5].

Reactive lymphocytosis is caused by various infectious and noninfectious stimuli, including viral infections such as Epstein-Barr virus, cytomegalovirus, HIV, measles, mumps, varicella, influenza, hepatitis A/B/C, and rubella, as well as certain bacterial infections like Bordetella pertussis, Bartonella henselae, Mycobacterium tuberculosis, Brucella, and Treponema pallidum [1].
Noninfectious causes include autoimmune diseases, medications (e.g., carbamazepine, vancomycin, allopurinol), stress reactions from trauma, acute cardiac ischemia, vigorous exercise, and smoking [1].
Persistent basophilia, defined as lasting more than 8 months, is always suggestive of a neoplastic hematologic disorder [2].

A left shift indicates an increase in circulating immature neutrophil precursors, such as bands, metamyelocytes, myelocytes, promyelocytes, and blasts, often associated with conditions like infection, inflammation, or stress [1][2].
It is usually seen on the peripheral blood smear when toxicity is present and may be accompanied by toxic changes like granulation, vacuolation, or dohle bodies in neutrophils [1][5].
A severe neutrophilia with a left shift is termed a leukaemoid reaction [2][3].
Monocytosis occurs in acute and chronic inflammatory conditions, including atherosclerosis and infections, as it results from systemic inflammation that recruits monocytes to inflammatory sites [4].
It can also be associated with reactive causes such as infections that lead to myelomonocytosis, mimicking leukemia [3].
Additionally, hypercholesterolemia stimulates monocyte levels, with lipid-lowering treatments reducing circulating monocytes, indicating a link between dyslipidemia and monocytosis [2].
A segmented neutrophil has two to five lobes connected by a filament [1][2].
The normal range for basophils in peripheral blood is ≤2% of leukocytes, with an absolute count upper limit of 0.1 × 10^9/L [1].
Cytoplasmic vacuoles in neutrophils are indicative of phagocytosis or autophagocytosis, often associated with severe bacterial infections or toxic states [3].
They can also be more numerous or larger than normal in toxic or septic conditions, and their presence may be linked to bacterial or yeast phagocytosis if the patient is septic [3][4].
Vacuolization is frequently observed in neutrophils during systemic inflammatory responses, especially in sepsis [2].

Cell identification and interpretation are subject to variability due to differences in laboratory methods, storage conditions, and preparation protocols, which can cause cytological lesions that overlap with cell anomalies related to COVID-19 [1].
Storage-induced changes, such as apoptosis in neutrophils and monocyte vacuolization, can develop over time and temperature, potentially affecting morphological assessment [1].
These factors contribute to the fragility and appearance of white blood cells on blood films, leading to potential misinterpretation or artifacts.

Interleukin-3 (IL-3) is the most potent growth factor for basophil differentiation and maturation, promoting their development from progenitor cells and supporting their viability and activation [1][2].
Other regulators include granulocyte/macrophage colony-stimulating factor (GM-CSF), IL-5, transforming growth factor-beta (TGF-β), and thymic stromal lymphopoietin (TSLP) [1][2].
These cytokines and growth factors contribute to increased basophil production and activity in various conditions.
A left shift indicates an increase in circulating neutrophil precursors such as bands, metamyelocytes, and myelocytes, which can be a response to infection or inflammation [1].

Toxic changes like granulation, vacuolation, and dohle bodies are seen in neutrophils during active infection or toxicity, regardless of maturity, but a predominance of immature forms suggests an ongoing process [4].

The presence of immature neutrophils, especially with toxic features, can be significant in diagnosing infections or marrow responses, but their maturity status alone does not alter the general interpretation of these features [1][4].
Monocytosis, or elevated monocyte counts, commonly occurs in acute and chronic inflammatory conditions, including atherosclerosis [3].
Inflammation and dyslipidaemia are key factors that promote the accumulation of classical CD14 ++ CD16 − monocytes in plaques, leading to pro-inflammatory macrophages [5].
Additionally, hypercholesterolaemia stimulates increased levels of monocytes and neutrophils in circulation, and treatment with lipid-lowering agents can decrease these counts [3].

Eosinophilia can be caused by primary mechanisms involving clonal expansion of eosinophils due to somatic mutations, or secondary mechanisms as a response to exogenous cytokines from conditions such as infections, allergic diseases, or malignancies [1][2].

Hematological disorders may involve intrinsic factors like neoplastic clones, or extrinsic factors like cytokine stimulation, with classifications including myeloid and lymphoid neoplasms with eosinophilia [3].
Medications can also induce eosinophilia, often as part of allergic drug reactions, including drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS) [4].

Parasites such as Trichinella spiralis, Fasciola hepatica, and schistosomiasis are associated with high eosinophil counts, often exceeding 1×10^9/l, and can cause symptoms like fever, myalgia, and abdominal pain [3][5].
Helminths like Strongyloides stercoralis and clonorchiasis may also lead to chronic eosinophilia [3][5].
The diagnosis often involves detailed history and laboratory testing due to the wide range of parasitic diseases that can cause eosinophilia [3][5].

Yes, drug reactions can cause eosinophilia and lead to end organ damage, especially in severe cases like drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms (DRESS), which involves multisystem manifestations and can be life-threatening [1][2].

DRESS typically presents weeks after drug initiation with symptoms such as fever, rash, facial swelling, and systemic involvement, and may result in long-term sequelae or death if not recognized and managed promptly [2].
The severity of eosinophilia and associated tissue damage depends on the individual case and the specific drug reaction involved.
Eosinophil counts exceeding 0.5 × 10^9/L are considered eosinophilia, with hypereosinophilia defined as counts ≥1.5 × 10^9/L [4][5].
Mild eosinophilia ranges from 0.5 to 1.49 × 10^9/L, moderate from 1.5 to 5.0 × 10^9/L, and severe above 5.0 × 10^9/L [4][5].

The significance of the count depends on the presence of organ damage and clinical context, with counts ≥1.5 × 10^9/L being particularly relevant for hypereosinophilia and hypereosinophilic syndromes [1][3][5].

Eosinophil granules contain a crystalline core with proteins such as major basic protein (MBP), eosinophil peroxidase (EPO), eosinophil-derived neurotoxin (EDN), and eosinophil cationic protein (ECP), along with a surrounding matrix that includes these cationic proteins and other mediators like cytokines, chemokines, and growth factors [1][2][4].
They also contain Charcot-Leyden crystal protein (galectin-10), which can crystallize and is associated with eosinophilic infiltration [1][2].
Small granules contain acid phosphatase and arylsulfatase, while secretory vesicles or microgranules contain receptors, adhesion molecules, and albumin [1].

Eosinophils and basophils are increased in response to allergic or inflammatory processes, particularly in advanced-stage COPD, where tissue inflammation and immune microenvironment changes occur [5].
The increase in these cells is associated with a type 2 immune response, as indicated by elevated GATA3 expression, which promotes eosinophil and basophil recruitment and activation [5].
Such increases reflect ongoing tissue inflammation and immune activity in the airways.
Neutropenia is most commonly caused by viral infections, medications such as azathioprine and cyclophosphamide, and hypersplenism [2].
Autoimmune mechanisms, including the generation of autoantibodies against neutrophils, can also contribute to neutropenia [2].
Additionally, functional defects involving immune complex deposition and inhibition of chemotactic factors may play a role [2].
A leukemoid reaction can be distinguished from CML by the absence of the Philadelphia chromosome or BCR::ABL1 fusion gene, which are present in CML [5].
Leukemoid reactions typically do not show the marked basophilia, myeloid immaturity, or splenomegaly seen in CML, and the white blood cell count is usually lower than in CML [2][3].
Additionally, the proportion of immature myeloid cells and dysplasia are key criteria; in CML, these features are more prominent, whereas in leukemoid reactions, they are generally absent [3].
Cytogenetic or molecular testing for BCR::ABL1 is essential for definitive differentiation.
A Pelger-Huet cell is a neutrophil with hyposegmented nuclei, often appearing as a single round (unilobed) or dumbbell-shaped (bilobed) nucleus, with mature chromatin and abundant cytoplasm [1][2].

Congenital Pelger-Huet cells show normal granulation and affect 50-90% of neutrophils, while pseudo or acquired Pelger-Huet cells may have hypogranulation and are associated with hematologic malignancies, infections, or drug effects, affecting 10-30% of neutrophils [1][2][3][4].
The condition is benign when congenital, with normal cell function, but pseudo Pelger-Huet may indicate underlying pathology.

A Dohle body is a pale blue, round or elongated cytoplasmic inclusion containing remnant ribosomal RNA (RNA) in parallel rows, often present in mature neutrophils and bands near the cell periphery [3][5].
They are non-specific and can appear in various conditions such as infections, pregnancy, cancer, and burns [3].
Dohle bodies are associated with toxic changes in neutrophils, which may also include toxic granulation and vacuolation [3].

Primary granules contain enzymes such as myeloperoxidase (MPO), serine proteases (including neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G), and antimicrobial peptides, and are present from the promyelocyte stage of neutrophil development [1][2].
Secondary granules contain enzymes like collagenase (MMP-1), lysozyme, lactoferrin, and NADPH oxidase, and appear in the myelocyte/metamyelocyte stage [2].

A large lymphocyte typically has a cell size of 9-12 microns, a high nucleus-to-cytoplasm ratio of about 4:1, and a round or indented nucleus with coarse, smudged chromatin; its cytoplasm is light to dark blue and may have indents from red blood cells [4][5].

A monocyte ranges from 7-18 microns, often with an eccentric nucleus that may be indented or folded, and has abundant, often vacuolated, pale blue cytoplasm with fine azurophilic granules; it also exhibits pseudopodia and vacuoles [4][5].
The monocyte's nucleus is usually irregular or folded, whereas the lymphocyte's nucleus is round or indented with coarser chromatin [4][5].

Reactive lymphocytes are typically heterogeneous in morphology, including various types such as Downey type I, II, and III cells, and often show simultaneous expansion of lymphocytes and monocytes [5].
Flow cytometry can help distinguish reactive from neoplastic lymphocytes by identifying clonal or abnormal populations, especially when morphological features are ambiguous [2][5].

In contrast, neoplastic lymphoproliferative disorders may present with monomorphous lymphocytes and require ancillary studies like immunohistochemistry, flow cytometry, and molecular tests for confirmation [3].
Recognizing clinical context and associated features is also important in the assessment.
An atypical lymphocyte is not necessarily the same as a reactive lymphocyte; terminology varies depending on the context.

In COVID-19, the term "atypical lymphocyte" is used to describe cells with heterogeneous morphology, often considered reactive or suspect reactive, but the ICSH recommends using "reactive lymphocytes" for benign, non-malignant cells [1][3].
Reactive lymphocytes can include various morphological subtypes, such as Downey types I, II, and III, which are associated with immune responses to infection [2].

Therefore, while many atypical lymphocytes are reactive, not all atypical lymphocytes are classified explicitly as reactive, and the terminology can overlap or differ based on the classification system used [1][2][3].
A monocyte nucleus can have variable shapes, including folds and kidney-shaped forms, with loose, lacy, violet chromatin [1].
It often appears irregular, and may contain nucleoli, although these are not always visible [1].
The chromatin is typically fine and diffuse, and the nucleus may be eccentrically located [1].

Monocytosis indicates CMML when it is persistent, with monocyte counts ≥ 0.5 × 10^9/L, constituting at least 10% of the white blood cell differential, and accompanied by evidence of clonality through somatic mutations or chromosomal aberrations [1][3].
Flow cytometry showing an increased proportion of classical monocytes (CD14+/CD16−) ≥ 94% can also support the diagnosis, especially when PB monocytosis is ≥ 1 × 10^9/L [4].
However, monocytosis alone is not sufficient, as reactive causes must be excluded, and other diagnostic criteria such as dysplasia and clonality are essential [2][3].
Basophil granules are metachromatic, staining pink or red with toluidine blue due to their high proteoglycan content [1].
They are typically large and dense, and their metachromatic property is characteristic, although toluidine blue cannot differentiate them from mast cell granules [1].
Specific esterase staining reacts with mast cell granules but not with basophilic granules, which can aid in differentiation [2].
Yes, reactive (non-clonal) basophilia can occur due to various causes, and persistent basophilia lasting more than 8 months is suggestive of a neoplastic hematologic disorder [3].

Basophils are normally produced in the bone marrow and can increase in response to certain cytokines such as interleukin-3, GM-CSF, IL-5, TGF-β, and TSLP, which regulate their development and differentiation [2][3].

A slide requires manual review when the blood film quality or stain quality is inadequate for accurate cell identification, or when morphological abnormalities are detected that necessitate detailed evaluation, such as in cases of suspected hematological pathology or abnormal differential counts [3][4].
Automated analyzers rely on high-quality slides, and traumatic morphological changes caused by automated slide makers can lead to errors, especially if performed by unskilled personnel [1][3].
Therefore, manual review is essential in situations where automated methods may be compromised or when specific morphological details are critical for diagnosis [3][4].
Prolonged storage of blood samples can lead to time-dependent changes in leukocyte morphology and counts, including a significant decrease in segmented neutrophils after 24 hours [1][3].

Neutrophils are considered short-lived cells that undergo apoptosis within approximately 24 hours in circulation, and their counts may decline over time, especially if the sample is not processed promptly [4].
Additionally, other leukocytes and blood cells, such as erythrocytes and platelets, may also undergo morphological changes after 12–24 hours, which could impact clinical assessments [5].

An absolute eosinophil count (AEC) measures the number of eosinophils per unit volume of blood, typically expressed as cells/mm³ or ×10⁹/L, and is used to define eosinophilia and hypereosinophilia [1][2][3][4].
A relative count refers to the percentage of eosinophils among total leukocytes or in differential counts, indicating the proportion of eosinophils relative to other white blood cells [2][3][4].
Both measures are important, but the diagnosis of eosinophilia often relies on the absolute count, while the relative count provides context within the total leukocyte population [2][4].
A neutrophil is a polymorphonuclear leukocyte that plays a key role in innate immunity by neutralizing and killing pathogens such as bacteria, fungi, and protozoans [2][3][5].
It accomplishes this through phagocytosis, degranulation releasing antimicrobial compounds, and generating reactive oxygen species (ROS) via enzymes like NADPH oxidase and MPO [1][2][3][4][5].
Additionally, neutrophils produce neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which capture and eliminate pathogens but often lead to neutrophil death [1][2][3][4].
A neutrophil extracellular trap (NET) is a web-like structure composed of decondensed nuclear chromatin and granular proteins such as neutrophil elastase, myeloperoxidase, and others [2][5].

NETs are formed as part of the innate immune response to trap, neutralize, and kill pathogens like bacteria, viruses, fungi, and parasites, and they can also be involved in sterile inflammation and tissue damage [2][5].

They may be expelled through various mechanisms, including a form of cell death called NETosis, or independently of cell death, resulting in structures that function in antimicrobial defense and potentially contribute to pathological processes [4][5].
Neutrophil granules contain a variety of molecules with proteolytic, antimicrobial, cytotoxic, and oxidative activities.
Primary granules include MPO, serine proteases such as neutrophil elastase and cathepsin G, and antimicrobial peptides like defensins [2].
Secondary granules contain enzymes such as lysozyme, lactoferrin, and NADPH oxidase, along with antimicrobial peptides like cathelicidin [2].
Tertiary granules harbor gelatinases (MMP-2 and MMP-9), cathepsin, and lipocalin 2 [2].

An eosinophil is a polymorphonuclear cell derived from hematopoietic precursors that plays a crucial role in defense against parasitic infections, primarily through the release of toxic granule proteins and antibody-dependent cytotoxic mechanisms [2][5].
They are also involved in modulating immune responses, tissue repair, and maintaining homeostasis, but can contribute to inflammation and tissue damage in eosinophil-associated diseases [3][5].
Eosinophils are primarily tissue-resident cells, especially abundant in mucosal tissues, where they influence homeostasis and immune responses [1][4].
Eosinophils can be damaging to tissue because they release toxic granule proteins, cytokines, and mediators that induce inflammation, tissue damage, fibrosis, and thrombosis [1][3].
When they undergo massive and persistent activation, their toxic content can harm the microenvironment and cause organ dysfunction [3].
This tissue damage is characteristic of hypereosinophilic syndromes and eosinophil-associated diseases [1][3].
Basophil granules contain proteoglycans that stain metachromatically, giving them a pink or red appearance with dyes like toluidine blue [4].
These granules can release proinflammatory cytokines, histamine, and other mediators that contribute to immune modulation, allergic responses, and inflammation [3].

Basophil granules stain so dark because they contain a large amount of proteoglycans that take up metachromatic stains, such as toluidine blue or methylene blue, resulting in pink or red coloration [1].

A basophil is a multifunctional hematopoietic cell derived from multipotent stem cells, primarily produced in the bone marrow, and characterized by metachromatic granules rich in histamine, proteoglycans, and inflammatory cytokines like IL-4 and IL-13 [4].
Unlike mast cells, basophils do not contain tryptase and have a short lifespan (<3 days) [4].

Morphologically, metachromatic granules in basophils react with specific esterase staining, and they express surface markers such as CD123, which is part of the IL-3 receptor, whereas mast cells carry tryptase and CD117, and their granules have different ultrastructural features, including four types of granules without a theta character [1].

Lymphocytes participate in cell-mediated immunity and can become activated to perform specific immune responses, as indicated by their ability to take part in cell-mediated immunity and their specific surface markers such as CD3, CD4, and CD8 [3].

Neutrophils, on the other hand, primarily neutralize pathogens through phagocytosis, release reactive oxygen species, and form neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), but they do not have the same capacity for adaptive, antigen-specific responses [1].

The segmented nucleus of a neutrophil is characteristic of polymorphonuclear leucocytes, with 2 to 5 lobes connected by a filament, which allows for flexibility and deformability as the cell navigates through narrow capillaries and tissue spaces [2][3].
This nuclear segmentation is a defining feature of mature neutrophils and is associated with their ability to migrate efficiently to sites of infection or inflammation [1].
